header: IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, PESHAWAR
Tahir Muhammad son of Nisar Muhammad, resident of
For appellant: M/s. Astaghfir Ullah, and
Research assistance: Riaz Aslam Daavi, SRO,
body: *** INAM ULLAH KHAN, J.- Through this consolidated judgment, this Court intends to dispose of Criminal Appeal No. 894-P/2025 (filed by appellant-convict Tahir Muhammad against his conviction and sentence), Criminal Revision No. 226-P/2025 (filed by complainant/legal heir Mashal Khan seeking enhancement of sentence), and Criminal Appeal No. 1116-P/2025 (filed by Mashal Khan against the acquittal of respondent Tahir Muhammad under Section 324 of PPC). All three connected matters emanate from and challenge the impugned judgment dated 15.09.2025, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-III, Swabi, in Sessions Case No. 49/SC of 2024 arising out of FIR No. 356, dated 05.06.2020, registered under Sections 302/324/34 Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (PPC) at Police Station Zaida, District Swabi.

2. Brief facts of the prosecution case are that on 05.06.2020, the complainant, Abbas Khan, brought the dead body of his maternal uncle, deceased Gohar Rehman, aged about 50/51 years and a resident of Village Zaida, with the help of his other relatives to the Casualty of Bacha Khan Medical Complex (BKMC), Shahmansoor, Swabi. He reported the matter to Zakir Khan, HC/Incharge Casualty, in the presence of the CMO, stating that he and his maternal uncle, Gohar Rehman, were travelling from Village Shahmansoor towards their village, Zaida. The motorcycle was being ridden by his maternal uncle, Gohar Rehman (deceased), while he was sitting on the pillion seat. They were reportedly followed by another motorcycle carrying their maternal cousins, Zahir Ali and Farman Ali. At about 11:20 a.m., when they reached the place of occurrence, co-accused Asad (acquitted) and Tahir (appellant) approached them from behind on a motorcycle. Asad was driving the motorcycle, while Tahir (appellant), who was armed with a firearm, was sitting on the pillion seat. Tahir (appellant) started firing at them with the intention to kill them. As a result of the firing, his maternal uncle lost control of the motorcycle and fell to the ground. During this time, co-accused Asad stopped the motorcycle, while Tahir (appellant) dismounted and started firing further, as a result of which his deceased maternal uncle sustained firearm injuries and died on the spot, whereas the complainant remained unhurt. Besides the complainant, the occurrence was also witnessed by Zahir Ali and Farman Ali, who were following them at the time of the occurrence. After committing the offence, the accused fled from the spot. The complainant stated that they could not do anything as they were empty-handed. The motive behind the occurrence was stated to be a previous blood-feud/enmity between the accused and the deceased, Gohar Rehman. The report of the complainant was verified by Zahir Ali. The complainant charged the accused for the commission of the offence.

3. After the commission of the alleged offence, as both accused evaded arrest, the prosecution submitted a complete challan against them under section 512 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1898 (CrPC), after completing the requisite formalities. During the proceedings under Section 512 CrPC, the co-accused, Asad, was arrested, and upon completion of the investigation into his involvement, a supplementary challan was submitted. Accused Asad was summoned and appeared before the Court, whereupon the provisions of Section 265-C CrPC were complied with. A formal charge was framed against accused Asad, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. During the trial, the prosecution examined five witnesses. Meanwhile, the learned defence counsel filed an application under Section 265-K CrPC. After hearing the arguments of Dy.PP for the State and learned defence counsel, accused Asad was acquitted of the charge levelled against him under Section 265-K CrPC.

4. Subsequently, on 21.04.2024, appellant Tahir Muhammad was arrested by SHO Farooq Khan (PW-1). After completion of investigation to his extent by Raz Muhammad SI (PW-12), a supplementary challan was submitted against him. Upon entrustment of the case, appellant Tahir Muhammad, being in judicial custody, was summoned and produced before the learned trial court. The provisions of Section 265-C CrPC were duly complied with by delivering copies of the police report and statements of witnesses to the appellant free of cost. Thereafter, on 03.07.2024, a formal charge under Sections 302/324/34 PPC was framed against the appellant, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

5. In order to substantiate its charges, the prosecution examined thirteen (13) witnesses. Upon conclusion of the trial and after hearing arguments from both sides, the learned trial Court vide impugned judgment dated 15.09.2025 convicted appellant Tahir Muhammad under Section 302(b)/34 PPC and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for life. The appellant was further directed to pay a compensation of Rs. 500,000/- (Rupees five hundred thousand) to the legal heirs of deceased Gohar Rehman within the meaning of Section 544-A CrPC, or in default of payment thereof, to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months. The benefit of Section 382- B CrPC was also extended to the appellant-convict. However, the appellant was acquitted of the charge under Section 324/34 PPC.

6. Feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment of conviction and sentence, appellant-convict Tahir Muhammad has preferred Criminal Appeal No. 894-P/2025, praying for setting aside his conviction and sentence and his consequential acquittal. On the other hand, Mashal Khan (son of the deceased) has filed Criminal Revision No. 226-P/2025, seeking enhancement of the appellant's sentence from life imprisonment to the normal penalty of death, as well as Criminal Appeal No. 1116-P/2025, assailing the acquittal of respondent/accused Tahir Muhammad of the charge under Section 324/34 PPC.

7. We have considered the arguments of learned counsel for the parties and examined the record with their assistance. The question is whether the evidence legally brought on record against this appellant establishes his participation in the occurrence beyond reasonable doubt. Under Article 117 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (QSO), the prosecution must prove the facts on which criminal liability is asserted.

8. Before undertaking a detailed appraisal of the evidence, it is appropriate to recall the settled principles governing the appreciation of evidence in criminal cases. Every criminal case must be decided on its own peculiar facts and circumstances, as no rigid or inflexible formula can govern the assessment of evidence in all situations. While the legal principles enunciated by the superior Courts are binding where applicable, observations made in the context of a particular factual situation must be understood in their proper perspective rather than applied mechanically to cases involving different circumstances. Ocular testimony, being direct evidence, must be assessed on its intrinsic worth, keeping in view the earliest version of the occurrence, the presence and natural conduct of the witnesses, their opportunity to observe the incident, the medical and forensic 117(1) Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist. (2) When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person.

Illustrations (a) A desires a Court to give judgment that B shall be punished for a crime which A says B has committed. A must prove that B has committed the crime. (b) A desires a Court to give judgment that he is entitled to certain land in the possession of B by reason of facts which he asserts, and which B denies to be true. A must prove the existence of those facts.

evidence, and the physical circumstances of the crime scene. In this regard, mere relationship of an eyewitness with the victim or deceased does not render his testimony unworthy of belief, nor does the absence of previous enmity with the accused necessarily establish his truthfulness. A related witness is not necessarily an interested witness; the latter is one who is motivated by some extraneous consideration, partisan interest or ulterior motive to falsely implicate the accused. The decisive consideration is whether the witness was genuinely present at the place of occurrence, had a reasonable opportunity to witness the incident, and has furnished a natural, consistent and probable account which inspires confidence when examined in the light of the surrounding circumstances. It is equally settled that evidence is to be weighed and not counted, as its quality rather than quantity determines its probative value. A conviction may, therefore, validly rest upon the testimony of even a solitary eyewitness, provided his evidence is trustworthy and inspires confidence. Conversely, where material doubts arise regarding the presence or account of a witness, prudence requires independent corroboration before reliance can safely be placed upon such testimony. It is also a settled principle that minor discrepancies, inconsistencies or omissions in the testimony of prosecution witnesses, which do not affect the substance of the prosecution case, are inconsequential. Human memory is not a photographic record of events; rather, recollection involves a process of reconstruction, which may naturally give rise to minor variations in the narration of an occurrence. Such variations, unless affecting the material particulars of the prosecution case, do not necessarily impair the credibility of a witness. What matters is whether the testimony, considered as a whole, remains consistent on material particulars and inspires confidence. Only those contradictions which strike at the root of the prosecution case or materially affect its credibility can undermine the evidentiary worth of the testimony. Above all, the burden of proving the charge beyond reasonable doubt rests upon the prosecution, which must establish its case on the strength of its own evidence. In evaluating the evidence, the Court must distinguish between minor and natural discrepancies and material infirmities which create reasonable doubt regarding the guilt of the accused. Such doubt must be real and rational, arising from the evidence or lack thereof, rather than imaginary, speculative or fanciful. If, upon a cumulative assessment of the record, even a single circumstance creates reasonable doubt in the mind of a prudent judge regarding the guilt of the accused, the benefit of that doubt must accrue to the accused as a matter of right and not of grace or concession. The judicial mind must, therefore, maintain a careful balance between unwarranted indulgence towards the accused and mechanical acceptance of a prosecution case affected by material infirmities.

9. On the touchstone of the foregoing settled principles of criminal jurisprudence, the present matter shall now be adjudged. The primary pillar of the prosecution narrative is the ocular account furnished by complainant Abbas Khan (PW- 10), who claimed to be riding pillion directly behind deceased Gohar Rehman during continuous, point-blank automatic firing and the subsequent violent crash of the motorcycle. A meticulous scrutiny of the physical circumstances reveals that PW-10 did not sustain a single firearm entry wound, grazing shot, bullet scratch, or physical abrasion. His subsequent effort during cross-examination to invent a fall injury or pain in his hand stands completely demolished by the contemporaneous record: Zakir Ali, IHC (PW-6), who scribed the report at BKMC Swabi, categorically admitted that PW-10 disclosed no injury whatsoever and no injury sheet was prepared. Where an eyewitness claims to occupy a position immediately behind the victim during a sustained automatic weapon ambush, escaping unscathed without a scratch pricks the judicial mind to the core and demonstrates that the witness was absent from the scene. It is correct that the mere absence of injury to an eyewitness does not, by itself, render his testimony unreliable or disprove his presence at the scene. A person may witness a firearm attack from close proximity and yet escape unhurt, depending on the direction of firing, his position and movements, and the person against whom the attack is directed. The Court cannot, therefore, presume that a witness must have sustained an injury merely because he claims to have been near the deceased. His presence must instead be assessed from the account he gives and its consistency with the surrounding circumstances and other evidence. However, the absence of injury may assume evidentiary significance when examined in conjunction with the nature, duration and manner of the alleged attack, the position occupied by the witness, and the other circumstances appearing on the record. In this regard, guidance may be drawn from the pronouncements of the superior Courts discussed hereinafter.

10. In Azmat Khan v. Ahmed Yar and others (1999 SCMR 2409), the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that the ocular account was hardly believable where the tractor had sustained bullet marks, yet its driver and the eyewitnesses escaped completely unhurt despite indiscriminate firing by a large number of assailants. In Rohtas Khan v. State (2010 SCMR 566), the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that where the accused had a motive against the complainant but caused him no injury despite his being within firing range, such circumstance supported the inference that the eyewitnesses were not present at the place of occurrence. In Iftikhar Ahmad alias Meena v. State (2026 SCMR 674), the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that where the deceased sustained multiple firearm injuries with corresponding exit wounds on his back, the presence of eyewitnesses on the pillion seat of his motorcycle would have been improbable without their sustaining injuries. The Court further found their claim of proceeding on foot, instead of accompanying the deceased on his motorcycle, to be unnatural and indicative of their absence from the place of occurrence. The relevant observations are reproduced herein below:

“...therefore, it was difficult for the said witnesses to justify their presence on the motorcycle of the deceased at the time of occurrence because in that case, they (PWs) should have also received injuries if they sitting on the pillion seat of the motorcycle of the deceased due to the bullets which went through and through from four (04) exit wounds on the back side of the body of the deceased...”

In Shah Hussain v. State and another (2024 PCrLJ 455), this Court held that where the complainant claimed to have been seated on the pillion seat of a motorcycle driven by the deceased at the time of the firearm attack, his escape without sustaining any injury, in the circumstances of the case, rendered his presence at the place of occurrence highly doubtful. The Court observed that, having regard to the direction of firing and the firearm injuries sustained by the deceased, the survival of the complainant unhurt, whether the firing was made from the front or the rear, was beyond comprehension. The relevant observations contained in paragraph 6 of the judgment are reproduced hereinbelow: “6. The core question for determination before us is that as to whether the prosecution has been able to establish the presence of complainant Muhammad Farooq at the spot with the deceased at the time of occurrence beyond shadow of reasonable doubt. In this case, as per FIR the deceased was riding the motorbike and the complainant was pillion with him. As per version of the complainant, they were proceeding from their house to Passani Bazar and on the way they were fired at by accused i.e. appellant Shah Hussain, Jehangir (acquitted co-accused) and Saeed Ullah (dead co-accused) who were already present on the spot duly armed with firearms. Admittedly, complainant/PW-6 is the sole eye-witness of the occurrence and there is no denial that conviction can be based on the testimony of a solitary eye-witness, as a rule of prudence, Court do not base a conviction on the evidence of a solitary eye-witness, unless that eyewitness is absolutely reliable or his evidence is corroborated by reliable evidence. If we look at the medical evidence i.e. the statement of the doctor and post mortem report Ex.PM the deceased has sustained 07 group entry wounds are on left back and right back of chest of the deceased while their corresponding exit wounds on the left front and right front of the chest. It is in the evidence of complainant/PW-6 that he spotted the accused while proceeding to Passani Bazar and the accused started firing at them. In the site plan prepared at the instance of the complainant, acquitted co-accused Jehangir and appellant Shah Hussain has been shown at point Nos.3 and 5 and i.e. in the front of the deceased and the complainant. If it is interpreted other way around and for the time being it is assumed that the firing was made from the back even in that situation the survival of the complainant was also impossible. In other words, whether firing is made from the front or back at the deceased, survival of the complainant with the deceased on the motorbike is beyond our comprehension and his presence cannot be believed in either situation...”

In Saddam v. State and others (2025 MLD 1644), this Court held that where the complainant and an eyewitness claimed to have been fired upon by the accused but escaped completely unhurt, such circumstance rendered their presence at the place of occurrence doubtful. The relevant portion of paragraph 10 of the judgment is reproduced hereinbelow:

“The complainant also disclosed that he and the eyewitness was fired at, but they escaped unhurt. Had the witnesses been present and had they been fired at, then there was hardly an occasion for them to escape unhurt, but the record suggests that neither they were fired at, nor they were present on the spot.”

In Liaqat Ali Khan v. State and another (2025 PHC 304), this Court held that where the complainant and an eyewitness claimed to have remained standing at their respective places during 4–5 minutes of indiscriminate Kalashnikov firing from a distance of approximately five paces, yet escaped without sustaining even a scratch, such unnatural conduct and improbable escape cast serious doubt on their presence at the place of occurrence. The relevant paragraph 18 of the judgment is reproduced hereinbelow:

“18. The prosecution case is that besides the deceased, the complainant and the eyewitness were also simultaneously fired at by two assailants with Kalashnikovs from a distance of around 05 paces. The firing continued for about 04 to 05 minutes, the complainant claimed, adding that they remained present at their respective places and did not move while the assailants were committing the gunshots at them. Notwithstanding this, neither the complainant nor the eyewitness received even a single scratch, let alone firearm entry wounds. Instead, both of them were fortunate enough to escape unhurt, despite standing like statues to the gunshots. It is imperative to note that the I.O, in his statement, admitted it correct that the walls surrounding the complainant had not bullet marks. In the circumstances, neither the conduct displayed by the complainant and the eyewitness appeals to a prudent mind, nor was their escape unhurt possible in the attending circumstances. This particular aspect of the case pricks our minds to the core. The case of Mst. Arbab Khatoon v. Imam Bakhsh and 03 others (2021 MLD 1286 Balochistan) has somewhat similar facts and circumstances, where it was observed:

Cr.A No 65-B/2023, Liaqat Ali Khan v. The State, decided on 11.02.2025 The witnesses were within the firing range of the accused/respondents that too when allegedly the accused were armed with pistols and Kalashnikovs, which were automatic weapons. So escaping unhurt of the witnesses does not appeal to the prudent mind despite the fact that the distance between the deceased, the witnesses and the accused/ respondents were given as 5/6 steps, from such a short distance how the witnesses remained safe.” In Shafqatullah v. State (2025 PHC 5679), this Court held that where three persons, including the deceased, the complainant and a minor, were travelling on the same motorcycle and the deceased sustained fatal firearm injuries, the complainant's claim that he and the minor escaped without sustaining even a scratch was inherently improbable and cast serious doubt on his presence at the place of occurrence. The relevant portion of paragraph 9 of the judgment is reproduced hereinbelow:

“He alleged that he alongwith his deceased brother and minor nephew were on motorcycle when the accused started firing by 12 repeater but the story is totally unbelievable because that the complainant party consisting three persons were on one and the same motorcycle, however, from the firing of 12 bore repeater how the complainant and the minor escaped unhurt as they did not receive a fire shot even a single scratch when they fell down from the motorcycle.”

In Muhammad Imran v. State (2020 YLR 1139, Para-15), the Lahore High Court, while invoking Article 129 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, held that where eyewitnesses, despite being within firing range, escaped completely unhurt although the assailants had the motive and opportunity to eliminate them, such conduct was contrary to the natural course of human behaviour and rendered their presence at the place of occurrence doubtful. Lastly, in Mst. Arbab Khatoon v. Imam Bakhsh and others (2021 MLD 1286, Paras 6-7), Cr.A No 223-B of 209, Shafqatullah V. The State, decided on 13.03.2025. the Balochistan High Court held that where eyewitnesses claimed to have remained within five to six steps of assailants firing with pistols and Kalashnikovs for two to three minutes, yet escaped completely unhurt, such circumstance did not appeal to a prudent mind and cast serious doubt on the prosecution version. Viewed in the light of the cited precedents, these circumstances cast doubt on the claim of complainant claimed presence at the place of occurrence and undermine the credibility of the ocular account.

11. Admittedly, the prosecution enjoys the discretion to produce such evidence as it considers necessary to substantiate its case; however, such discretion does not absolve it of the consequences of withholding material eyewitnesses or other natural witnesses of the occurrence without any plausible justification. It is well settled that the unexplained nonproduction of such witnesses may attract an adverse inference against the prosecution under Article 129(g) of the QSO 1984, that had they been examined, their testimony would have been unfavourable to the prosecution case. In Muhammad Nasir Butt and others v. State and others (2025 SCMR 662), the Hon'ble Supreme Court drew an adverse inference from the prosecution's failure to produce an injured passerby and a cited eyewitness, observing that had they been examined, their testimony would not have supported the prosecution version. Similarly, in Rasheed Ahmad alias Sheeda v. State (2026 SCMR 798), the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that nonproduction of the deceased's husband and children, who were considered natural witnesses of the occurrence, amounted to withholding the best evidence and justified drawing an adverse inference under Article 129(g), ibid. The same principle was reiterated in Umer Draz and another v. State and others (2026 SCMR 1185), wherein the unexplained abandonment of two female family eyewitnesses, allegedly injured during the occurrence, was held to constitute withholding of material evidence, warranting an adverse inference against the prosecution. Likewise, in Saddam v. State and others (2025 MLD 1644), this Court drew an adverse inference where a cited eyewitness, being the maternal cousin of the complainant, was abandoned as won over after submitting an affidavit denying his own presence as well as that of the complainant at the place of occurrence. A similar view was taken by this Court in Zubair Ahmad and others v. State and another (2026 YLR 1614), wherein non-production of a material witness, who had identified the deceased's body, was considered sufficient to attract an adverse inference under Article 129(g) of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. Thus, where the prosecution withholds a material and naturally available witness without satisfactory explanation, the Court may, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, presume that the evidence of such witness, if produced, would have been unfavourable to the prosecution.

12. In the present case, the FIR expressly names Zahir Ali and Farman Ali, maternal cousins of the complainant, as eyewitnesses to the occurrence, who allegedly followed the deceased on a separate motorcycle and also attested the murasila. However, during trial, the prosecution abandoned both witnesses, tendering the boilerplate plea that they were 'won over'. The withholding of material eyewitnesses specifically cited in the FIR, particularly in a case involving a capital charge where the presence of the solitary complainant as an eyewitness is itself shrouded in serious doubt, deprives the Court of material corroborative evidence. Such unexplained non-production warrants the drawing of an adverse inference against the prosecution under Article 129, Illustration (g), of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, that had these witnesses been examined, their testimony would have been unfavourable to the prosecution case.

13. The prosecution asserted that the complainant (PW-10) and the cited eyewitnesses accompanied the dead body of the deceased to BKMC, Swabi, immediately after the occurrence. However, the contemporaneous official record does not reflect their participation in bringing or identifying the dead body. The post-mortem examination report (Ex.PM) records that the dead body was brought by Constable Kashif (No. 1052) and identified by Fazal-e-Subhan, whereas the inquest report mentions Ali Askar and Fazal-e-Subhan (PW-8) as the persons who identified the deceased. Admittedly, neither the complainant nor the cited eyewitnesses are named in the relevant identification columns of these documents. It must, however, be appreciated that identification of a dead body may lawfully be undertaken by persons other than eyewitnesses of the occurrence, and the mere absence of an eyewitness's name from such record does not, by itself, conclusively establish his absence from the place of occurrence. Nevertheless, where the prosecution specifically asserts that the complainant and other eyewitnesses accompanied the deceased to the hospital immediately after the incident, their omission from the contemporaneous hospital and inquest records is a circumstance requiring explanation, particularly when their claimed presence at the place of occurrence is otherwise disputed. Had the complainant or the cited eyewitnesses identified the dead body at the time of post-mortem examination, their names could reasonably have been expected to appear in the relevant record. In this regard, guidance may be drawn from Mst. Sughra Begum and another v. Qaiser Pervez and others (2015 SCMR 1142), wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court, in paragraph 15, considered the absence of the purported eyewitnesses' names from the contemporaneous medico-legal and inquest records, despite their claim of having accompanied the deceased to the hospital, as a material circumstance casting doubt upon their presence at the place of occurrence. A similar view was expressed by the Lahore High Court in Muhammad Farooq v. State and another (2023 PCrLJ 1771), wherein neither the complainant nor the cited eyewitnesses had identified the deceased's body or attested the inquest report, which was instead identified and attested by other persons. The relevant portion is reproduced hereinbelow:

“Perusal of Inquest Report (Ex.PN) further reflects that neither the complainant nor cited eyewitnesses identified the dead body of the deceased of the case and in Column No.4 of the Inquest Report, names of the persons identifying the dead body of the deceased are mentioned as “Nasir and Shafique”; similarly, Inquest Report was neither attested by the complainant nor cited eyewitnesses rather same was attested by Munir Ahmad and Muhammad Siddique. Nutshell of the above discussion is that testimonies of the complainant and aforementioned both cited eyewitnesses are neither confidence inspiring nor trustworthy, hence, cannot be relied in this case of capital punishment.”

In the present case, although the omission of the name of the complainant from the post-mortem and inquest reports is not conclusive proof of his absence from the hospital or the place of occurrence, it assumes significance when considered alongside the other infirmities already discussed. The said documents do not furnish independent support to the prosecution assertion that the complainant accompanied the deceased immediately after the occurrence. Consequently, this circumstance, viewed cumulatively with the doubts surrounding the claimed presence of the complainant as a pillion rider on the motorcycle at the time of occurrence, further weakens the credibility of the ocular account.

14. The ocular narrative alleges that while the motorcycle was moving at speed, appellant Tahir Muhammad opened fire, causing driver Gohar Rehman to lose control and crash violently onto the road. The motorcycle was taken into possession vide recovery memo Ex.PW-9/4; however, the said memo is conspicuously silent regarding its physical condition, particularly whether it bore any damage or marks consistent with the alleged violent crash. In violent motorcycle crashes caused by gunfire, significant physical marks—such as scraping, broken indicators, bent handlebars, or shattered headlights—are inevitably produced. Here, the prosecution produced no inspection report, or photographic evidence showing physical damage to the vehicle. When evaluated alongside PW-10's complete lack of injury, the absence of physical vehicle damage refutes the sequence of events portrayed by the prosecution. Where the prosecution asserts that a motorcycle met with a violent crash following a firearm attack, the condition of the motorcycle, the existence or otherwise of corresponding damage, and the injuries, if any, sustained by its occupants constitute relevant circumstances for examining the credibility of the ocular account. It is pertinent to mention here that the Investigating Officer ought to have properly photographed the place of occurrence, the physical condition of the motorcycle, the bloodstains and the three spent cartridge cases reflected in recovery memo Ex.PW-9/2, so as to preserve the physical evidence and facilitate verification of the alleged mode and manner of occurrence. However, no such photographic documentation was undertaken by the Investigating Officer, which constitutes a significant omission in the investigation. In Muhammad Farooq v. State and another (2023 PCrLJ 1771), the Lahore High Court, while scrutinizing the prosecution evidence, attached significance to the failure of a cited eyewitness to furnish particulars of the motorcycle on which he allegedly accompanied the deceased. Applying the same principle of careful scrutiny to the present case, the alleged violent fall of the motorcycle, the complainant's escape without sustaining even a scratch or abrasion, the absence of any corresponding physical damage to the motorcycle, and the failure of the Investigating Officer to photograph the place of occurrence and the physical condition of the motorcycle, when considered cumulatively, constitute material circumstances casting serious doubt upon the credibility of the prosecution version regarding the alleged mode and manner of occurrence.

15. It is by now a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that where an eyewitness makes material and dishonest improvements in his testimony with a view to strengthening the prosecution case, explaining away material deficiencies or bringing his account into conformity with other evidence on record, such testimony loses its credibility and cannot safely be made the basis of conviction. In Muhammad Khan and others v. State (1999 SCMR 1220), the Hon'ble Supreme Court, in paragraph 15 of the judgment, held that it would be unsafe to rely upon ocular evidence which had been moulded, changed and improved step by step so as to fit in with other evidence on record. Similarly, in Khalid Mehmood and another v. State and another (2021 SCMR 810), the Hon'ble Supreme Court, while examining material improvements introduced by the prosecution eyewitnesses regarding the circumstances of the occurrence, the weapons carried by the accused and the injuries sustained by the deceased, found their claimed presence at the place of occurrence doubtful. The same principle was reiterated by this Court in Liaqat Ali Khan v. State and others (2025 PHC 304), wherein, in paragraph 15, reliance was placed upon the pronouncements of the Hon'ble Supreme Court concerning dishonest improvements made to bring ocular testimony into conformity with medical evidence or otherwise strengthen the prosecution case. Thus, a distinction must be maintained between minor discrepancies arising from ordinary human error and material improvements deliberately introduced to overcome deficiencies in the prosecution case. While the former may not necessarily impair the credibility of a witness, the latter, particularly when affecting the essential features of the occurrence, render the ocular account unsafe for reliance.

16. In the present case, the complainant (PW-10), in his initial murasila (Ex.PA/1), described the weapon of offence merely as “Aslaha Atishin” (firearm), without specifying its nature, type or calibre. However, while appearing before the learned trial Court approximately four years after the occurrence, he introduced a material improvement by asserting that he had specifically described the weapon as a “Kalashnikov” before the police, although no such description finds mention in his initial version. This subsequent improvement assumes particular significance in view of the alleged recovery of a Kalashnikov from the appellant nearly four years after the occurrence, thereby raising a serious question as to whether the complainant attempted to bring his ocular account into conformity with the recovery evidence. It is, no doubt, a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the FIR or murasila is not an encyclopaedia of the occurrence, nor is it expected to contain every minute detail thereof, its primary object being to convey information regarding the commission of a cognizable offence and set the machinery of law into motion. While finer details of the occurrence may legitimately emerge during investigation, material facts which were within the knowledge of the complainant at the time of reporting the occurrence would ordinarily be expected to find mention in his earliest account. A distinction must, therefore, be drawn between the subsequent disclosure of incidental particulars and the introduction of a material fact which, if actually known to the complainant, would ordinarily have formed part of his initial version. The effect of such omission must, however, be assessed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, its explanation, if any, and whether the subsequent disclosure amounts to a material improvement affecting the credibility of the prosecution case. This Court is also mindful that an ordinary person cannot be expected to possess technical expertise regarding the caliber, make or precise specifications of a firearm. However, a Kalashnikov, being a relatively large, distinctive and commonly recognizable firearm, is ordinarily distinguishable from other weapons without requiring any specialized knowledge. Therefore, where the complainant professes to have witnessed the occurrence at close range and subsequently asserts that he had specifically identified the weapon as a Kalashnikov, the omission of such description from his initial murasila assumes material significance and calls for a plausible explanation. It is to be noted that a previous omission or statement may be used to test the credibility of a witness where the relevant portion is duly put to him and the contradiction is established in accordance with law. Not every omission constitutes a material contradiction, and not every subsequent elaboration amounts to a deliberate improvement. The Court must determine whether the omitted detail was material in the circumstances and whether its later introduction affects the reliability of the witness's account. In the present case, the description of the alleged weapon assumes importance because the prosecution subsequently relied upon the recovery of a particular firearm and sought to connect it with the crime empties. The complainant's later assertion that he had already disclosed the weapon to be a Kalashnikov is not supported by the earliest recorded version, as described by PW-6. In the absence of any satisfactory explanation, the subsequent introduction of this specific description, particularly after the alleged recovery of a similar weapon, casts doubt upon the spontaneity and credibility of the ocular account. Such a material improvement, if duly established through confrontation with the previous statement in accordance with Article 140 of the QSO 1984, would considerably impair the credibility of the complainant and render his testimony unsafe for implicit reliance.

17. Another pivotal aspect requiring detailed judicial scrutiny is the alleged recovery of the weapon of offence and its subsequent forensic evaluation. According to the prosecution, Ilyas, SI (PW-11), recovered three crime empties 140. Cross-examination as to previous statements in writing. A witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing or reduced into writing, and relevant to matters in question, without such writing being shown to him, or being proved; but, if it is intended to contradict him by the writing, his attention must, before the writing can be proved, be called to those parts of it which are to be used for the purpose of contradicting him.

of 7.62 mm calibre (marked C-1 to C-3) and one missed cartridge (marked M) from Point-C of the place of occurrence on 05.06.2020 through recovery memo Ex.PW-9/2. Nearly four years thereafter, on 21.04.2024, a 7.62 mm Kalashnikov rifle along with ten live rounds was allegedly recovered from the possession of appellant Tahir Muhammad. Although Fazle Khaliq, ASI (PW-4), claimed that the recovered weapon was sealed in Parcel No. 4, Aqil, FC (PW-7), a marginal witness to the recovery memo, categorically admitted during crossexamination that the Kalashnikov was not sealed at the place of recovery. PW-5, Muhammad Fayyaz, ASI, and PW-12, Raz Muhammad, SI, also admitted during cross-examination that the Kalashnikov was not in a sealed condition. More importantly, the crime empties secured in 2020 and the Kalashnikov allegedly recovered in 2024 were dispatched together to the Forensic Science Laboratory and received there on 02.05.2024. The prosecution failed to establish an unbroken chain of custody or furnish any explanation regarding the safe preservation of the crime empties in police station custody during the intervening period of nearly four years. These deficiencies assume greater significance in view of the negative FSL report, which categorically establishes that crime empties C-1 to C-3 were not fired from the recovered Kalashnikov. Thus, the forensic examination establishes no ballistic link between the recovered weapon and the crime empties secured from the place of occurrence. A negative FSL report utterly fails to connect the weapon with the crime scene and provides zero corroboration to a doubtful ocular account. It is well settled that a recovery which is not supported by reliable connecting evidence cannot, by itself, establish the guilt of an accused. In the circumstances of this case, the recovery and ballistic evidence fail to provide a dependable link between the appellant and the commission of the offence. Consequently, the alleged recovery, being merely corroborative in nature, loses its evidentiary significance and is of no assistance to the prosecution in connecting the appellant with the commission of the offence.

18. The evidentiary value of a recovered firearm, when relied upon as corroborative evidence, depends upon its forensic connection with the crime empties recovered from the place of occurrence, as well as proof of safe custody and transmission of the recovered articles. In Iftikhar Ahmad alias Meena v. State (2026 SCMR 674), the Hon'ble Supreme Court, in paragraph 7, held that where the crime empties did not match the recovered pistol, the alleged recovery became inconsequential for the prosecution case. Similarly, in Muhammad Nasir Butt and others v. State and others (2025 SCMR 662), paragraphs 8 and 9, the Hon'ble Supreme Court took into consideration the negative FSL report and the absence of independent witnesses to the recovery while disbelieving the same. The Lahore High Court, in Muhammad Farooq v. State (2023 PCrLJ 1771), also held that the recovery of a firearm was of no assistance to the prosecution where the crime empties recovered from the spot were not found to have been fired from that weapon. As regards safe custody and transmission, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ali Sher and others v. State (2008 SCMR 707), paragraphs 10 and 11, held that the unexplained retention of crime empties at the police station for over three weeks and their subsequent dispatch to the FSL along with the recovered weapons deprived the recoveries of their corroborative value. The same principle was followed by this Court in Shah Hussain v. State and another (2024 PCrLJ 455), wherein prolonged and unexplained retention of crime empties, followed by their transmission with the recovered weapons, rendered the ballistic report unreliable due to the possibility of substitution. Likewise, in Saddam v. State and others (2025 MLD 1644), this Court declined to rely upon the recovery where safe custody and transmission of the recovered articles were not satisfactorily established. Applying these principles to the present case, the failure to seal the Kalashnikov at the place of recovery, the unexplained deficiencies in the chain of custody and, more importantly, the negative FSL report establishing that crime empties C-1 to C-3 were not fired from the recovered Kalashnikov, deprive the alleged recovery of its corroborative value. Consequently, the recovery becomes inconsequential and is of no assistance to the prosecution in connecting the appellant with the commission of the offence.

19. The autopsy conducted by Lady Dr. Afshan (PW-13) confirms that deceased Gohar Rehman died of fatal firearm injuries. However, medical evidence is purely confirmatory in nature regarding the cause of death, locale of injuries, and nature of weapon. Medical evidence cannot identify who pulled the trigger, nor can it cure the fundamental defects, contradictions, and improbabilities in PW-10's ocular narrative. It is a settled principle that medical evidence is essentially corroborative in nature; it may establish the cause of death, nature and location of injuries and the kind of weapon used, but cannot, by itself, identify the assailant. In Muhammad Masood alias Mithu v. State and others (2025 SCMR 888), the Hon'ble Supreme Court, in paragraph 9, expressly reiterated this distinction, holding that a postmortem report does not establish the identity of the person responsible for the occurrence. Conversely, in Iftikhar Kiyani alias Khara v. State (2025 SCMR 1360), paragraph 7, the Hon'ble Supreme Court recognized the corroborative value of medical evidence where the ocular account was otherwise trustworthy and confidence-inspiring. Thus, while the medical evidence in the present case establishes the homicidal death of the deceased through firearm injuries, it does not independently establish the appellant's identity or participation in the occurrence. Once the presence and credibility of the complainant as an eyewitness are rendered doubtful, the medical evidence, being corroborative in nature, cannot by itself cure the deficiencies in the ocular account or furnish an independent basis for sustaining the conviction.

20. The prosecution laid heavy emphasis on appellant Tahir Muhammad's four-year absconsion. While absconsion is a relevant corroborative circumstance under Article 21 of the QSO1984, it is well settled that absconsion cannot form the sole basis of conviction, nor can it cure inherent defects, false improvements, or negative FSL reports in the prosecution case. It is, however, well settled that abscondence, though a relevant circumstance, is merely corroborative in nature and cannot, by itself, establish the guilt of an accused or cure the inherent defects in the prosecution case. In Muhammad Khan 21. Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct. (1) Any fact is relevant which shows or constitutes a motive or preparation for any fact in issue or relevant fact.

(2) The conduct of any party, or of any agent to any party, to any suit or proceeding, in reference to such suit or proceeding, or in reference to any fact in issue therein or relevant thereto, and the conduct of any person an offence against whom is the subject of any proceeding, is relevant, if such conduct influences or is influenced by any fact in issue or relevant fact, and whether it was previous or subsequent thereto. Explanation 1. — The word “conduct” in this clause does not include statements, unless those statements accompany and explain acts other than statements but this explanation is not to affect the relevancy of statements under any other Article of this Order.

Explanation 2. —When the conduct of any person is relevant, any statement made to him or in his presence and hearing, which affects such conduct, is relevant. and another v. State (1999 SCMR 1220), the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that abscondence is neither necessarily indicative of guilt nor sufficient, by itself, to sustain a conviction. In Qaisar Khan and others v. The State and others (2009 SCMR 471), the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that abscondence, though a relevant corroborative circumstance, cannot by itself sustain a conviction and must be considered in conjunction with the substantive ocular and circumstantial evidence. The same principle was reiterated in Rohtas Khan v. State (2010 SCMR 566), wherein it was held that abscondence is merely a suspicious circumstance which must be considered alongside substantive evidence and not in isolation. In Khalid Mehmood alias Khaloo v. State (2022 SCMR 1148), the Hon'ble Supreme Court again held that abscondence cannot be treated as independent proof of the commission of an offence. More recently, in Muhammad Masood alias Mithu v. State and others (2025 SCMR 888), paragraph 8, the Hon'ble Supreme Court reaffirmed that mere abscondence cannot form the sole basis of conviction or compensate for deficiencies in the prosecution evidence. Likewise, this Court in Shafqatullah v. State (2025 PHC 5679), paragraph 16, held that abscondence can only lend corroboration to otherwise reliable substantive evidence. Applying these principles to the present case, where the ocular account suffers from material infirmities and the alleged recovery of the weapon has failed to provide forensic corroboration, the appellant's abscondence, even if established, cannot rehabilitate the prosecution case or independently connect him with the commission of the offence. Consequently, no decisive evidentiary significance can be attached to this circumstance.

21. Motive is not a sine qua non for sustaining a conviction where reliable and confidence-inspiring ocular evidence establishes the charge. Nevertheless, where the prosecution specifically alleges a motive, its failure to prove the same is a circumstance requiring consideration in the overall appraisal of evidence. In the present case, Amir Abdur Rehman Khan (PW-9), brother of the deceased, did not mention any motive or previous enmity between the parties in his examination-inchief. Likewise, the complainant (PW-10) referred to previous enmity only during examination-in-chief, without producing any supporting evidence. The Investigating Officer, Ilyas, SI (PW-11), neither investigated nor explained the alleged motive and merely produced a copy of an earlier FIR (Ex.PW- 11/6), without elucidating its relevance to the occurrence. Significantly, the learned trial Court itself acknowledged, in paragraph 18 of the impugned judgment, that motive had not been established with certainty. In Mst. Nazia Anwar v. The State and others (2018 SCMR 911), paragraph 4, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that where the prosecution asserts a motive but fails to prove it, such failure may operate against the imposition of the death sentence, although the conviction may still be maintained if otherwise supported by reliable evidence establishing guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Similarly, in Saddam v. The State and others (2025 MLD 1644), paragraph 13, this Court observed that although absence or weakness of motive does not, by itself, warrant acquittal, it assumes significance once the ocular account is found unreliable. Thus, while failure to establish motive is not independently fatal to the prosecution case, in the present circumstances, where the ocular account is already attended by material doubts and lacks dependable corroboration, the unproved motive constitutes an additional circumstance weighing against the prosecution.

22. Having examined the testimony of the complainant (PW-10) in the light of the entire prosecution evidence, we find that his account does not inspire the requisite confidence. His claimed presence as a pillion rider on the motorcycle at the time of occurrence remains doubtful in view of his escape without any injury, the absence of contemporaneous medical evidence concerning his alleged hand injury or pain, the inconsistency in his statements in that regard, and the nonproduction of the other cited eyewitnesses. The subsequent improvement regarding the description of the weapon further affects the credibility of his testimony. Moreover, the alleged recovery of the Kalashnikov has failed to establish any forensic connection with the crime empties recovered from the place of occurrence, while the condition of the motorcycle does not furnish the expected physical corroboration of the occurrence in the manner narrated. These circumstances, when considered alongside the discrepancies emerging from the contemporaneous record, raise serious doubts regarding the presence of PW-10 at the place of occurrence. We are conscious that minor discrepancies or natural variations in recollection do not necessarily impair otherwise reliable testimony. However, the infirmities identified in the present case are not confined to peripheral matters but strike at the very foundation of the ocular account.

23. In these circumstances, the prosecution has failed to establish the presence of PW-10 with the deceased at the place of occurrence beyond reasonable doubt, rendering his claim to have witnessed the occurrence unsafe for reliance. In Muhammad Khan and another v. The State (1999 SCMR 1220), paragraph 15, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the entire evidence and surrounding circumstances must be examined in their proper perspective and that an inherently improbable or materially improved ocular account cannot safely form the basis of conviction. Similarly, in Mst. Sughra Begum and another v. Qaiser Pervez and others (2015 SCMR 1142), the Hon'ble Supreme Court emphasized the importance of examining the intrinsic worth of ocular testimony in the light of the surrounding circumstances, particularly where the claimed presence of eyewitnesses is doubtful. The principles enunciated in these judgments are fully attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present case.

24. It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the prosecution must establish its case beyond reasonable doubt and that even a single circumstance creating reasonable doubt in the mind of a prudent person regarding the guilt of an accused is sufficient to entitle him to acquittal, such benefit being a matter of right and not of grace or concession. This principle has consistently been reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Muhammad Mansha v. The State (2018 SCMR 772, para. 4), Sikandar Ali alias Bhola v. The State (2025 SCMR 552, para. 10), Muhammad Siddique and another v. The State and others (2026 SCMR 783, para. 13), Shahbaz alias Gillo v. The State and others (2026 SCMR 1349, para. 11), Ali Imran and others v. The State and another (2026 SCMR 1370, para. 10), Munir Ahmad and 3 others v. The State and others (2026 SCMR 1498, para. 13) and Mehmood Khan and others v. The State (2026 SCMR 1606, para. 8). In the present case, the cumulative effect of the infirmities discussed above renders the prosecution version doubtful on material particulars. The prosecution has, therefore, failed to discharge its burden of proving the charge against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt, and he is consequently entitled to the benefit thereof.

25. For the foregoing reasons, we find that the prosecution has failed to prove the charge against the appellant, Tahir Muhammad, beyond reasonable doubt, thereby entitling him to the benefit of doubt. Consequently, Criminal Appeal No. 894-P/2025 is allowed, the impugned judgment dated 15.09.2025, passed by the learned trial Court, is set aside, and the appellant, Tahir Muhammad, is acquitted of the charge. He shall be released forthwith, if not required to be detained in any other case. As a necessary consequence of the acquittal of the appellant, Criminal Revision No. 226-P/2025, seeking enhancement of his sentence, and Criminal Appeal No. 1116- P/2025, challenging his acquittal, are also dismissed.
26. The above are the detailed reasons for the short order of even date.
